newsitem.title: FINLAND: Simulated nuclear accident begins in Finland.
newsitem.headline: Simulated nuclear accident begins in Finland.

text.p: Hundreds of experts in Europe and beyond began an emergency exercise on Thursday based on a simulated accident at the Loviisa nuclear power plant on the south coast of Finland.
The exercise is in two parts. In the first phase the plant develops a serious problem and a leak of radioactive material is feared; this is followed by the actual leak.
Experts will try to predict the direction of radioactive fallout based on actual and forecast wind direction in the region.
By early Thursday morning, the first phase of the exercise had begun, said Eero Oksanen, senior inspector at the Finnish Centre for Radiation and Nuclear Safety.
"The first information we got from (the plant) was that they thought things are not going right," Oksanen said by telephone.
"But we are having a meeting right now so I'm afraid I can't talk for very long."
The simulated accident will trigger practice alerts in 27 other countries, mainly in Europe but also in Japan and South Korea.
Weather and nuclear experts in other Nordic countries and in France, Germany, Britain and beyond will be monitoring the liklihood and extent of radioactive contamination.
Later, planners will consider whether they made the correct decisions to deal with the emergency.
Weatherman Mikko Jantti said a cold front over southern Finland was expected to disperse by midday local time and winds would strengthen towards the south east.
This would send simulated radioactive fallout towards Russia and the Baltic states.
The test assumes the plant's operators may try to play down the danger.

This aspect will be particularly significant for Japan, which decided at the last minute to join in the exercise after Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto ordered an investigation into the cover-up of the nation's worst nuclear accident last month.
A group of firefighters in the central Finnish town of Kuopio plan to simulate the general public, bombarding emergency services with telephone calls. Troublemakers are not ruled out.
A special Internet web site will carry simulated real-time media cover of the incident, including audio and text press releases and reports by a dummy real-time news agency.
Access to the Web site is protected by a password to ensure it does not get overloaded and to prevent any public alarm.
The plan of the exercise can be viewd on web page http://www.intermin.fi/sm/pelastus.
The exercise is part of a two-year programme set up by the Nuclear Energy Agency, part of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
